topic: cross-lingual pretrained models; representation sharing; transfer evaluation
status: within-study ablation pattern; broader replication needed
claim: In one controlled bilingual masked-language-model study across English-to-French/Russian/Chinese XNLI, NER, and dependency parsing, removing shared lexical anchors produced modest average changes (about −1.1 XNLI, −2.4 NER, and −0.9 parsing), whereas separating the bottom six Transformer layers caused much larger average drops (−22.6, −38.7, and −17.8). Extra anchors still helped more for distant pairs, and domain mismatch particularly harmed NER. Thus token overlap alone is not a sufficient explanation of the measured transfer; shared parameters and corpus domain are important competing levers in this experimental setup.

sources.title: Emerging Cross-lingual Structure in Pretrained Language Models
locators: §4.3/Table 1: separate embeddings and bottom Transformer layers
§5: discussion of anchor points and parameter sharing

interpretation: This records the measured ablation pattern, not a claim that shared vocabulary is generally unimportant or that upper-layer sharing alone causes multilinguality. The no-anchor condition retains shared prediction parameters; the experiments use bilingual models and three tasks/language-pair settings.
falsifiable_question: Across modern multilingual models, language pairs, and tasks, how much transfer variance is explained by lexical-anchor quantity, shared-layer depth, and pretraining-domain match when compute, corpus size, and language exposure are controlled? Do anchor effects grow systematically with typological distance or lower-resource status?
primary_outcome: Zero-shot task performance and calibration on held-out language pairs; secondary outcomes include sample-efficiency curves and representation alignment, with separate estimates by task and typological distance.
counterevidence_and_caveats: Extra anchors improve some distant-language results by more than three points, so lexical anchors are not irrelevant.
The no-anchor condition keeps shared softmax/prediction parameters and does not eliminate all cross-language parameter sharing.
Only bilingual models, three tasks, and three English-to-target pairs were evaluated; this is not a modern multilingual-scale replication.
NER corpora and domain conditions differ; data-source effects may interact with task.
Global novelty is unconfirmed.
suggested_design: Use a factorial ablation varying shared vocabulary fraction, shared-layer depth, corpus-domain match, and language exposure under equal compute/data budgets. Include related and distant language pairs, low-resource languages, multiple task families, and held-out languages; preregister the interaction terms.

topic: membership and attribute inference; privacy-risk measurement
claim: Yeom et al. connect generalization error to membership-inference advantage and show a simple loss-threshold attack performs competitively on selected linear/tree/CNN settings. But attribute-inference results differ by target (success on tested IWPC genomic attributes, failure on the Netflix movie-rating target), and their constructed colluding malicious training algorithm attains membership advantage ≥0.98 on sufficiently large CNNs with only small predictive-accuracy losses. The evidence supports using generalization gap as a risk signal in some benign settings, not as a stand-alone privacy guarantee or universally calibrated risk score.

sources.title: Privacy Risk in Machine Learning: Analyzing the Connection to Overfitting
locators: §§2–3 and theorems: overfitting/generalization and membership inference
§6.2/Table 1: membership attack precision/recall on image benchmarks
§§3.4 and 6.4: colluding training algorithm and CNN evaluation

interpretation: The counterexample is a deliberately malicious/colluding construction, not evidence that typical benign training silently leaks this much. The practical results depend on dataset, target attribute, model capacity, and attacker knowledge; direct attack evaluation remains necessary.
falsifiable_question: Across benign and adversarial training pipelines, do generalization gap, algorithmic stability, and attribute influence jointly calibrate membership and attribute attacks on held-out datasets, or are there repeatable low-gap/high-leakage regions missed by gap-only triage?
primary_outcome: Attack advantage/precision/recall and attribute-inference advantage, reported separately from test accuracy and generalization gap; assess proxy calibration on datasets not used to fit thresholds.
counterevidence_and_caveats: The selected membership experiments do show generalization behavior is a strong predictor in several tested settings.
Attribute inference can fail even when membership results are informative; target influence matters.
The strongest low-gap counterexample requires a malicious colluding learning algorithm and sufficiently large networks.
Attackers may need training-loss/distribution knowledge or model-inversion assumptions.
Datasets and architectures are selected historical benchmarks; no deployed-system prevalence is estimated.
Global novelty is unconfirmed.
suggested_design: For each dataset/model pair, evaluate multiple benign and deliberately adversarial training algorithms; measure membership and attribute attacks under matched attacker access, record stability/generalization/influence separately, and test calibration on held-out tasks. Predefine low-gap/high-attack cases as proxy failures.

topic: mutation testing; learned code transformations; test adequacy
status: single-study metric decomposition; external project-level test remains open
claim: A learned mutation study trained on roughly 2.3 million fixed-to-buggy Java transformation pairs reports exact reconstruction rates ranging from 9% to 45% across model variants and high lexical/syntactic correctness. However, some variants also produce substantial bad-prediction fractions (up to 54% in Table II), and the authors assess behavioral difference by inspecting methods outside their full system context. Therefore syntactic validity and similarity to historical bugs should not be treated as interchangeable with executable, behavior-changing, test-useful mutants.

sources.title: Learning How to Mutate Source Code from Bug-Fixes
locators: §IV RQ3: manual behavior evaluation by author judges

interpretation: This is an evaluation-gap hypothesis, not a conclusion that the generated mutants are invalid. The paper does manually assess a sample and reports real-bug resemblance; full project compilation/execution and test utility were not established by the cited headline syntax metric.
falsifiable_question: When evaluated in original project context at equal generation budgets, what fraction of learned mutants compile, produce behavior-changing failures, and yield tests that detect plausible faults compared with standard and domain-specific mutation operators? Does syntax-validity rank correlate with test-detection utility?
primary_outcome: Separate rates for parse/compile success, behavior change, kill rate, project-context validity, and test-generation yield, with manual blinded review of a sample.
counterevidence_and_caveats: Exact buggy-code reconstruction reaches 45% for one specialized model and syntactic correctness is high; learned mutants may be valuable.
The reported 9–45% values vary substantially by model and dataset cluster.
Manual behavior review uses multiple author judges, although method-level isolation may misclassify system behavior.
The study focuses on Java and mostly short methods; large commits were filtered out.
Global novelty is unconfirmed.
suggested_design: Run all generated mutants in their original repositories, enforce successful build and test execution, and compare against standard operators using matched mutation counts and runtime. Add held-out repositories, seeded faults, blinded behavior review, and report all funnel denominators from generated to test-killed.

status: numerical demonstration with acknowledged local minima
claim: A proximal-operator path-planning paper reports scalable-looking convergence and approximately 2× eight-core speedup on a synthetic 3D scenario, with similar objective values across 1,000 random initializations for that case. The authors explicitly acknowledge local minima, and the evaluation is primarily synthetic/demo-based. The evidence therefore motivates measuring initialization-sensitive feasibility and solution quality, rather than implying a global-optimum or real-robot guarantee.

sources.title: Proximal Operators for Multi-Agent Path Planning
locators: §5: Java numerical experiments, CONF1 scaling and 1,000 initializations
§5: six landmark toy scenarios and 10-agent/approximately 100-landmark demonstration

interpretation: The paper's numerical evidence is positive within its tested scenarios; absence of real hardware validation in that experiment does not show the planner fails in deployment. The research opportunity is to quantify the gap between optimizer objective and robust, dynamically feasible plans across broader conditions.
falsifiable_question: Across shared multi-agent planning instances with varied obstacle density, dynamics, and initialization, how often do proximal methods return collision-free, dynamically feasible plans, and how much do restart policy and core count change success rate and objective gap?
primary_outcome: Feasibility/constraint-violation rate, runtime, objective gap to lower bound, and across-seed variance, with real-robot or high-fidelity simulation validation as a separate stage.
counterevidence_and_caveats: The paper reports similar objective values across 1,000 initializations on CONF1 and encouraging results on its demonstrations.
The authors acknowledge local minima and propose better initial-point strategies as future work.
Results come from a Java numerical implementation on synthetic scenarios; they do not certify failure or success on hardware.
The collision/trajectory model and smoothing approximation may not transfer unchanged across robot dynamics.
Global novelty is unconfirmed.
suggested_design: Benchmark methods on common 2D/3D multi-agent instances across seeds, density, obstacles, and dynamic constraints; keep tuning separate from test instances. Report feasibility, objective lower-bound gap, runtime scaling, and paired per-instance failures; then validate selected cases in high-fidelity simulation/hardware.
